claim: Pancreatic cancer has a high mortality rate due to metastasis.
source: Pancreatic cancer has a high mortality rate due to metastasis.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about pancreatic cancer outcomes.

claim: KRAS is mutated in most pancreatic cancer patients.
source: Whereas KRAS is mutated in most pancreatic cancer patients, controlling KRAS or its downstream effectors has not been succeeded clinically.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about KRAS mutations in pancreatic cancer.

claim: Controlling KRAS or its downstream effectors has not been succeeded clinically.
source: Whereas KRAS is mutated in most pancreatic cancer patients, controlling KRAS or its downstream effectors has not been succeeded clinically.
evidence: This reflects current clinical knowledge about therapeutic challenges.

claim: ARL4C is a small G protein whose expression is induced by the Wnt and EGF–RAS pathways.
source: ARL4C is a small G protein whose expression is induced by the Wnt and EGF–RAS pathways.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: ARL4C is frequently overexpressed in pancreatic cancer patients.
source: In the present study, we found that ARL4C is frequently overexpressed in pancreatic cancer patients
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Localization of ARL4C to invasive pseudopods is required for cancer cell invasion.
source: we found that ARL4C is frequently overexpressed in pancreatic cancer patients and showed that its localization to invasive pseudopods is required for cancer cell invasion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: IQGAP1 was identified as a novel interacting protein for ARL4C.
source: IQGAP1 was identified as a novel interacting protein for ARL4C.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry and immunoprecipitation data.

claim: ARL4C recruited IQGAP1 and its downstream effector, MMP14, to invasive pseudopods.
source: ARL4C recruited IQGAP1 and its downstream effector, MMP14, to invasive pseudopods.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence and functional assays.

claim: Specific localization of ARL4C, IQGAP1, and MMP14 was the active site of invasion, which induced degradation of the extracellular matrix.
source: Specific localization of ARL4C, IQGAP1, and MMP14 was the active site of invasion, which induced degradation of the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is supported by DQ-collagen degradation assays and imaging data.

claim: Subcutaneously injected antisense oligonucleotide against ARL4C into tumor-bearing mice suppressed metastasis of pancreatic cancer.
source: Moreover, subcutaneously injected antisense oligonucleotide against ARL4C into tumor-bearing mice suppressed metastasis of pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo mouse experiments.

claim: ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling is activated at invasive pseudopods of pancreatic cancer cells.
source: These results suggest that ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling is activated at invasive pseudopods of pancreatic cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Pancreatic cancer has a 5 year survival of only 5%.
source: Pancreatic cancer is extremely aggressive and exhibits poor prognosis, with a 5 year survival of only 5 % (Klein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Klein, 2013.

claim: Most pancreatic cancer-related deaths are due to metastatic disease.
source: Most pancreatic cancer-related deaths are due to metastatic disease, and more than 80 % of patients have either locally advanced or metastatic disease (Hidalgo, 2010; Klein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hidalgo, 2010 and Klein, 2013.

claim: More than 80% of pancreatic cancer patients have either locally advanced or metastatic disease.
source: Most pancreatic cancer-related deaths are due to metastatic disease, and more than 80 % of patients have either locally advanced or metastatic disease (Hidalgo, 2010; Klein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hidalgo, 2010 and Klein, 2013.

claim: KRAS mutations are considered an initiating event in pancreatic ductal cells.
source: Genome sequencing analysis has revealed the mutational landscape of pancreatic cancer and KRAS mutations are considered an initiating event in pancreatic ductal cells (Collins et al., 2012; Waddell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2012 and Waddell et al., 2015.

claim: ARL4C is a member of the ADP-ribosylation factor (ARF)-like protein (ARL) family.
source: ARL4C is a member of the ADP-ribosylation factor (ARF)-like protein (ARL) family, which belongs to the ARF protein subgroup of the small GTP-binding protein superfamily (Engel et al., 2004; Matsumoto et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Engel et al., 2004; Matsumoto et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2009.

claim: Cytohesin2/ARNO has been identified as a direct effector protein of ARL4C.
source: Cytohesin2/ARF nucleotide-binding site opener (ARNO), a GDP/GTP exchange factor of ARF family proteins, has been identified as a direct effector protein (Hofmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hofmann et al., 2007.

claim: ARL4C is expressed through activation of Wnt–β-catenin and EGF–RAS signaling.
source: ARL4C is expressed through activation of Wnt–β-catenin and EGF–RAS signaling and plays important roles in both epithelial morphogenesis and tumorigenesis (Matsumoto et al., 2017; Matsumoto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Matsumoto et al., 2017 and Matsumoto et al., 2014.

claim: ARL4C plays important roles in both epithelial morphogenesis and tumorigenesis.
source: ARL4C is expressed through activation of Wnt–β-catenin and EGF–RAS signaling and plays important roles in both epithelial morphogenesis and tumorigenesis (Matsumoto et al., 2017; Matsumoto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Matsumoto et al., 2017 and Matsumoto et al., 2014.

claim: Aberrant activation of the Wnt–β-catenin and/or EGF–RAS pathways are frequently observed in various types of cancers.
source: Because aberrant activation of the Wnt–β-catenin and/or EGF–RAS pathways are frequently observed in various types of cancers, ARL4C is indeed expressed in a number of cancers (Fujii et al., 2015; Fujii et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujii et al., 2015 and Fujii et al., 2016.

claim: ARL4C is expressed in a number of cancers.
source: Because aberrant activation of the Wnt–β-catenin and/or EGF–RAS pathways are frequently observed in various types of cancers, ARL4C is indeed expressed in a number of cancers (Fujii et al., 2015; Fujii et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujii et al., 2015 and Fujii et al., 2016.

claim: In colon and lung cancer cells, ARL4C promotes cell proliferation through ARF6, RAC, RHO, and YAP/TAZ.
source: In colon and lung cancer cells, ARL4C promotes cell proliferation through ARF6, RAC, RHO, and YAP/TAZ.
evidence: This is based on prior research findings.

claim: In liver cancer cells, ARL4C promotes cell proliferation through phosphatidylinositol three kinase δ (PI3Kδ).
source: On the other hand, in liver cancer cells, ARL4C promotes cell proliferation through phosphatidylinositol three kinase δ (PI3Kδ) (Harada et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harada et al., 2019.

claim: ARL4C activates different downstream pathways in a cancer cell context-dependent manner.
source: Thus, ARL4C would activate different downstream pathways in a cancer cell context-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different mechanisms observed in different cancer types.

claim: IQGAP1 is a well-characterized member of the IQGAP family and a fundamental regulator of cytoskeletal function.
source: Mammalian IQGAP1 is a well-characterized member of the IQGAP family and a fundamental regulator of cytoskeletal function (Briggs and Sacks, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Briggs and Sacks, 2003.

claim: IQGAP1 is highly expressed in tumor lesions and suggested to be involved in cancer cell metastasis.
source: IQGAP1 is highly expressed in the tumor lesions and suggested to be involved in cancer cell metastasis (Johnson et al., 2009; Sakurai-Yageta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2009 and Sakurai-Yageta et al., 2008.

claim: ARL4C bound to IQGAP1 and recruited IQGAP1 and MMP14 to invasive pseudopods in a PIP3-dependent manner.
source: Here, we show that ARL4C bound to IQGAP1 and recruited IQGAP1 and membrane type1-matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP, also called MMP14) (Sakurai-Yageta et al., 2008) to invasive pseudopods in a phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3)-dependent manner and accelerated invasion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ARL4C bound to IQGAP1 and recruited IQGAP1 and MMP14 to invasive pseudopods and accelerated invasion.
source: Here, we show that ARL4C bound to IQGAP1 and recruited IQGAP1 and membrane type1-matrix metalloproteinase (MT1-MMP, also called MMP14) (Sakurai-Yageta et al., 2008) to invasive pseudopods in a phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3)-dependent manner and accelerated invasion.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ARL4C antisense oligonucleotide suppressed the lymph node metastases of pancreatic cancer cells orthotopically implanted into the pancreas of immunodeficient mice.
source: In addition, ARL4C antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) suppressed the lymph node metastases of pancreatic cancer cells orthotopically implanted into the pancreas of immunodeficient mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo mouse experiments.

claim: The ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling axis promotes pancreatic cancer aggressiveness.
source: These results suggest that the ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling axis promotes pancreatic cancer aggressiveness and that ARL4C is a novel molecular target for the treatment of pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: ARL4C is a novel molecular target for the treatment of pancreatic cancer.
source: These results suggest that the ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling axis promotes pancreatic cancer aggressiveness and that ARL4C is a novel molecular target for the treatment of pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and therapeutic potential.

claim: High expression of ARL4C was observed in 47 cases (82%) of 57 PDAC patients.
source: High expression of ARL4C was observed in 47 cases (82%), but minimally detected in non-tumor regions of pancreatic ducts (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ARL4C was minimally detected in non-tumor regions of pancreatic ducts.
source: High expression of ARL4C was observed in 47 cases (82%), but minimally detected in non-tumor regions of pancreatic ducts (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A significant difference was observed between low and high ARL4C expression based on perineural invasion.
source: A significant difference was observed between low and high ARL4C expression based on perineural invasion (Supplementary file 1 table 1).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data analysis.

claim: Perineural invasion is considered as one of the causes of the recurrence and metastasis after pancreatic resection.
source: Because the perineural invasion is considered as one of the causes of the recurrence and metastasis after pancreatic resection (Liang et al., 2016), ARL4C expression may be correlated with the ability of cancer cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2016.

claim: ARL4C expression may be correlated with the ability of cancer cell invasion.
source: Because the perineural invasion is considered as one of the causes of the recurrence and metastasis after pancreatic resection (Liang et al., 2016), ARL4C expression may be correlated with the ability of cancer cell invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation with perineural invasion.

claim: ARL4C expression was correlated with decreased overall survival.
source: Consistently, ARL4C expression was correlated with decreased overall survival (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ARL4C is highly expressed in tumor tissue than in non-diseased tissue.
source: Analysis of TCGA and GTEx datasets revealed that ARL4C is highly expressed in tumor tissue than in non-diseased tissue (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of public datasets shown in Figure 1C.

claim: High expression of ARL4C indicated a poor prognosis in TCGA dataset.
source: In addition, when ARL4C high and low expression groups were separated based on the top 75 % of mRNA values of ARL4C in TCGA dataset, high expression of ARL4C indicated a poor prognosis (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Higher ARL4C expression is an independent prognostic factor.
source: Univariate and multivariate analysis revealed that higher ARL4C expression is an independent prognostic factor (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: High expression of ARL4C is correlated with the aggressiveness and poor prognosis of pancreatic cancer.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that high expression of ARL4C is correlated with the aggressiveness and poor prognosis of pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence presented.

claim: ARL4C was highly expressed in PANC-1 and S2-CP8 cells.
source: In cultured pancreatic cancer cell lines, ARL4C was highly expressed in PANC-1 and S2-CP8 cells and it was barely detected in BxPC-3 cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ARL4C was barely detected in BxPC-3 cells.
source: In cultured pancreatic cancer cell lines, ARL4C was highly expressed in PANC-1 and S2-CP8 cells and it was barely detected in BxPC-3 cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The MEK inhibitors PD184161 and U0126 decreased ARL4C expression in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells.
source: Consistent with the previous results with IEC6 rat intestinal epithelial cells and colorectal and lung cancer cells (Fujii et al., 2015; Matsumoto et al., 2014), the MEK inhibitors PD184161 and U0126 and siRNAs for β-catenin and KRAS decreased ARL4C expression in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F-H.

claim: siRNAs for β-catenin and KRAS decreased ARL4C expression in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells.
source: Consistent with the previous results with IEC6 rat intestinal epithelial cells and colorectal and lung cancer cells (Fujii et al., 2015; Matsumoto et al., 2014), the MEK inhibitors PD184161 and U0126 and siRNAs for β-catenin and KRAS decreased ARL4C expression in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F-H.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of KRAS and β-catenin further suppressed ARL4C expression.
source: In addition, simultaneous knockdown of KRAS and β-catenin further suppressed ARL4C expression (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: ARL4C is expressed in pancreatic cancer cells through activated RAS–MAP kinase and Wnt–β-catenin pathways.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that ARL4C is expressed in pancreatic cancer cells through activated RAS–MAP kinase and Wnt–β-catenin pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data with inhibitors and siRNAs.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 has been shown to inhibit growth of xenograft tumors induced by colon and lung cancer cells.
source: ARL4C ASO-1316 has been shown to inhibit growth of xenograft tumors induced by colon and lung cancer cells (Harada et al., 2019; Kimura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harada et al., 2019 and Kimura et al., 2020.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 had little effect on sphere formation of pancreatic cancer cell.
source: However, ARL4C ASO-1316 had little effect on sphere formation of pancreatic cancer cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B and B) and did not induce cell death, which is assessed by propidium iodide (PI) staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 did not induce cell death.
source: However, ARL4C ASO-1316 had little effect on sphere formation of pancreatic cancer cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B and B) and did not induce cell death, which is assessed by propidium iodide (PI) staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by PI staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 inhibited the migratory and invasive abilities with dominant effects on invasion.
source: ARL4C ASO-1316 inhibited the migratory and invasive abilities with dominant effects on invasion (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by Boyden chamber assay data shown in Figures 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Inhibition of migratory and invasive abilities by ARL4C ASO was not observed in the cells expressing ARL4C-GFP ectopically.
source: Inhibition of migratory and invasive abilities by ARL4C ASO, targeting the non-coding region of ARL4C mRNA, was not observed in the cells expressing ARL4C-GFP ectopically (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figures 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ARL4C could be involved in migration and invasion of pancreatic cancer cells.
source: Thus, ARL4C could be involved in migration and invasion of pancreatic cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ASO knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Control S2-CP8 cells invaded into type I collagen, while ARL4C ASO decreased invasive ability.
source: Whereas control S2-CP8 cells invaded into type I collagen, ARL4C ASO decreased invasive ability (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by 3D gel invasion assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: When the collagen concentration was reduced, S2-CP8 cells invaded irrespective of ARL4C knockdown.
source: When the collagen concentration was reduced, S2-CP8 cells invaded irrespective of ARL4C knockdown (Figure 2G), suggesting that their invasive ability is not required for cells to move into the ECM when collagen fiber-formed 3D net structures are sparse.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Invasive ability is not required for cells to move into the ECM when collagen fiber-formed 3D net structures are sparse.
source: When the collagen concentration was reduced, S2-CP8 cells invaded irrespective of ARL4C knockdown (Figure 2G), suggesting that their invasive ability is not required for cells to move into the ECM when collagen fiber-formed 3D net structures are sparse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells invade regardless of ARL4C at low collagen concentrations.

claim: ARL4C-tdTomato accumulated in the tips of invasive pseudopods in 3D gel invasion assay.
source: Furthermore, in the 3D gel invasion assay ARL4C-tdTomato accumulated in the tips of invasive pseudopods (Figure 2H; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: ARL4C dynamically appeared and disappeared in the pseudopods, but it did not accumulate in the cytoplasm.
source: Fluorescence intensities of ARL4C-tdTomato in the edges of the pseudopods and cytoplasm (20 μm away from the tip of pseudopod), respectively, were measured over time, and then the intensities were plotted as a function of time. The results indicate that ARL4C dynamically appeared and disappeared in the pseudopods, but it did not accumulate in the cytoplasm (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Most invasive pseudopods were located in the angle of –45 to +45 degrees in the polar histogram, suggesting that invasive pseudopods play a role in purposeful directional invasion.
source: Using time-lapse imaging the angle of pseudopods to the direction of cell movement towards FBS was observed. Most of them were located in the angle of –45 to +45 degrees in the polar histogram, suggesting that invasive pseudopods play a role in purposeful directional invasion (Figure 2I; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by angular analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Protease-induced fluorescence dequenching was detected in the collagen fibers crossing the tips of the pseudopods but not in the cell body.
source: Protease-induced fluorescence dequenching was detected in the collagen fibers crossing the tips of the pseudopods but not in the cell body (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by DQ-collagen imaging data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Protease activity was decreased when ARL4C was depleted.
source: Protease activity was decreased when ARL4C was depleted (Figure 2K), suggesting that ARL4C is involved in degradation of the ECM through its localization to the tips of invasive pseudopods and plays an important role in the invasion of pancreatic cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by DQ-collagen quantification shown in Figure 2K.

claim: ARL4C is involved in degradation of the ECM through its localization to the tips of invasive pseudopods.
source: Protease activity was decreased when ARL4C was depleted (Figure 2K), suggesting that ARL4C is involved in degradation of the ECM through its localization to the tips of invasive pseudopods and plays an important role in the invasion of pancreatic cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protease activity data.

claim: ARL4C plays an important role in the invasion of pancreatic cancer cells.
source: Protease activity was decreased when ARL4C was depleted (Figure 2K), suggesting that ARL4C is involved in degradation of the ECM through its localization to the tips of invasive pseudopods and plays an important role in the invasion of pancreatic cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: ARL4C did not bind to cytohesin2 in S2-CP8 cells.
source: In S2-CP8 cells, ARL4C did not bind to cytohesin2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and knockdown of cytohesin2 had no effect on the migratory or invasive ability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of cytohesin2 had no effect on the migratory or invasive ability.
source: In S2-CP8 cells, ARL4C did not bind to cytohesin2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and knockdown of cytohesin2 had no effect on the migratory or invasive ability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by migration and invasion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cytohesin2 was distributed throughout the cytosol in S2-CP8 cells, whereas it was localized to the cell periphery of HeLaS3 cells.
source: Furthermore, cytohesin2 was distributed throughout the cytosol in S2-CP8 cells, whereas it was localized to the cell periphery of HeLaS3 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ARL4C ASO did not affect RAC1 activity in S2-CP8 cells.
source: Whereas ARL4C ASO inhibited RAC1 activity in A549 cells (Fujii et al., 2015), the ASO did not affect RAC1 activity in S2-CP8 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RAC1 activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ARL4C knockdown did not inhibit nuclear import of YAP/TAZ in pancreatic cancer cells.
source: Although ARL4C induces the nuclear import of YAP/TAZ in HCT116 cells (Harada et al., 2019), ARL4C knockdown did not inhibit it in pancreatic cancer cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by YAP/TAZ localization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Cytohesin2 neither functions downstream of ARL4C nor is involved in migration or invasion of pancreatic cancer cells.
source: These results suggest that cytohesin2 neither functions downstream of ARL4C nor is involved in migration or invasion of pancreatic cancer cells and prompted us to explore an uncharacterized effector protein of ARL4C.
evidence: This is an inference based on the negative results with cytohesin2.

claim: Ectopically expressed and endogenous ARL4C were associated with endogenous IQGAP1 in S2-CP8 cells.
source: Ectopically expressed and endogenous ARL4C were associated with endogenous IQGAP1 in S2-CP8 cells (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: ARL4C-FLAG-HA and ARL4CQ72L-FLAG-HA formed a complex with GFP-IQGAP1 to the similar levels, but ARL4CT27N-FLAG-HA showed diminished binding to GFP-IQGAP1 in X293T cells.
source: ARL4C-FLAG-HA and ARL4CQ72L-FLAG-HA formed a complex with GFP-IQGAP1 to the similar levels, but ARL4CT27N-FLAG-HA showed diminished binding to GFP-IQGAP1 in X293T cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ARL4C and IQGAP1 accumulated to invasive pseudopods at endogenous level in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells under Matrigel-coated 2D culture conditions.
source: Using another anti-ARL4C antibody for the immunocytochemical study (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B), ARL4C and IQGAP1 were shown to accumulate to invasive pseudopods at endogenous level in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells under Matrigel-coated 2D culture conditions (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Colocalization of ARL4C and IQGAP1 at invasive pseudopods was observed in 94% of cells with ARL4C accumulation to the pseudopods.
source: Colocalization of ARL4C and IQGAP1 at invasive pseudopods was observed in 94 % of cells with ARL4C accumulation to the pseudopods.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data.

claim: In 3D culture conditions, IQGAP1 was found at the tips of invasive pseudopods, similar to ARL4C-tdTomato.
source: In 3D culture conditions, IQGAP1 was found at the tips of invasive pseudopods, similar to ARL4C-tdTomato (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: IQGAP1 siRNA inhibited the migratory and invasive abilities in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells.
source: IQGAP1 siRNA inhibited the migratory and invasive abilities in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells, and the cells expressing GFP-IQGAP1 were resistant to IQGAP1 siRNA (Figure 3G and H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by migration and invasion assay data shown in Figures 3G-H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Cells expressing GFP-IQGAP1 were resistant to IQGAP1 siRNA.
source: IQGAP1 siRNA inhibited the migratory and invasive abilities in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells, and the cells expressing GFP-IQGAP1 were resistant to IQGAP1 siRNA (Figure 3G and H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figures 3G-H.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of ARL4C and IQGAP1 decreased the invasive ability, but the inhibitory degree was similar to that induced by knockdown of either ARL4C or IQGAP1.
source: Simultaneous knockdown of ARL4C and IQGAP1 decreased the invasive ability, but the inhibitory degree was similar to that induced by knockdown of either ARL4C or IQGAP1 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: IQGAP1 and ARL4C regulate invasion in identical signaling pathways.
source: Thus, IQGAP1 and ARL4C regulate invasion in identical signaling pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-additive effect of double knockdown.

claim: IQGAP1 was highly expressed in 31 of 57 PDAC patients (54%).
source: IQGAP1 was highly expressed in 31 of 57 PDAC patients (54%) (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: IQGAP1 expression correlated with decreased overall survival.
source: Although higher expression of IQGAP1 was not associated with clinical parameters (Supplementary file 1 table 3), IQGAP1 expression correlated with decreased overall survival (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Expression of ARL4C mRNA in pancreatic cancer patients is positively correlated with that of IQGAP1 mRNA.
source: TCGA dataset revealed that expression of ARL4C mRNA in pancreatic cancer patients is positively correlated with that of IQGAP1 mRNA (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Of 47 PDAC patients with high ARL4C expression, IQGAP1 was highly expressed in 27 patients.
source: Of 47 PDAC patients with high ARL4C expression, IQGAP1 was highly expressed in 27 patients (Supplementary file 1 table 4).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data analysis.

claim: Higher expression of ARL4C in the patients positive for IQGAP1 was associated with perineural invasion.
source: Higher expression of ARL4C in the patients positive for IQGAP1 was associated with perineural invasion (Supplementary file 1 table 4).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data analysis.

claim: Overall survival was significantly decreased in the order of low ARL4C/low IQGAP1, high ARL4C/low IQGAP1, and high ARL4C/high IQGAP1.
source: Overall survival was significantly decreased in the order of low ARL4C/low IQGAP1, high ARL4C/low IQGAP1, and high ARL4C/high IQGAP1, although the result of low ARL4C/high IQGAP1 could not conclude because of the small case numbers (n = 2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Simultaneous expression of ARL4C and IQGAP1 would be correlated with aggressiveness of pancreatic cancer.
source: Thus, simultaneous expression of ARL4C and IQGAP1 would be correlated with aggressiveness of pancreatic cancer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the survival analysis.

claim: ARL4CG2A-GFP and ARL4CΔPBR-GFP were not accumulated at invasive pseudopods where cortactin was present, but distributed throughout the cytosol.
source: In contrast to ARL4C-GFP, ARL4CG2A-GFP and ARL4CΔPBR-GFP were not accumulated at invasive pseudopods where cortactin was present, but distributed throughout the cytosol (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Both ARL4CG2A and ARL4CΔPBR mutants severely decreased the binding activity to GFP-IQGAP1.
source: In contrast to ARL4C-GFP, ARL4CG2A-GFP and ARL4CΔPBR-GFP were not accumulated at invasive pseudopods where cortactin was present, but distributed throughout the cytosol (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C), and both mutants severely decreased the binding activity to GFP-IQGAP1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Both ARL4CG2A-GFP-Cterm and ARL4CΔPBR-GFP-Cterm were localized to invasive pseudopods where cortactin was present.
source: The KRAS C-terminal region was fused to the ARL4C mutants, which were referred to as ARL4C-GFP-Cterm. Both ARL4CG2A-GFP-Cterm and ARL4CΔPBR-GFP-Cterm were localized to invasive pseudopods where cortactin was present (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ARL4CG2A-FLAG-HA-Cterm formed a complex with GFP-IQGAP1, but ARL4CΔPBR-FLAG-HA-Cterm did not.
source: However, although ARL4CG2A-FLAG-HA-Cterm formed a complex with GFP-IQGAP1, ARL4CΔPBR-FLAG-HA-Cterm did not (Figure 4D), suggesting that membrane localization of ARL4C is not sufficient for its binding to IQGAP1.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Membrane localization of ARL4C is not sufficient for its binding to IQGAP1.
source: However, although ARL4CG2A-FLAG-HA-Cterm formed a complex with GFP-IQGAP1, ARL4CΔPBR-FLAG-HA-Cterm did not (Figure 4D), suggesting that membrane localization of ARL4C is not sufficient for its binding to IQGAP1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential binding of membrane-localized mutants.

claim: The PBR is necessary for ARL4C to associate with IQGAP1, as well as for recruiting ARL4C to invasive pseudopods.
source: Taken together, the PBR is necessary for ARL4C to associate with IQGAP1, as well as for recruiting ARL4C to invasive pseudopods.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant analysis.

claim: The localization of IQGAP1 to invasive pseudopods was lost in ARL4C KO cells, but not vice versa.
source: The localization of IQGAP1 to invasive pseudopods was lost in ARL4C KO cells, but not vice versa (Figure 4E and F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4E-F and supplementary figures.

claim: In ARL4C KO cells, ARL4C-GFP and ARL4CG2A-GFP-Cterm rescued the recruitment of IQGAP1 to the plasma membrane, unlike ARL4CG2A-GFP, ARL4CΔPBR-GFP, and ARL4CΔPBR-GFP-Cterm.
source: In ARL4C KO cells, ARL4C-GFP and ARL4CG2A-GFP-Cterm rescued the recruitment of IQGAP1 to the plasma membrane, unlike ARL4CG2A-GFP, ARL4CΔPBR-GFP, and ARL4CΔPBR-GFP-Cterm (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: For IQGAP1 to be recruited to invasive pseudopods, the localization of ARL4C to the plasma membrane and the binding to IQGAP1 through the PBR might be necessary.
source: Therefore, for IQGAP1 to be recruited to invasive pseudopods, the localization of ARL4C to the plasma membrane and the binding to IQGAP1 through the PBR might be necessary.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments with different mutants.

claim: Inhibition of invasive ability by ARL4C ASO-1316 was cancelled by expression of ARL4CG2A-GFP-Cterm but not by that of ARL4CG2A-GFP, ARL4CΔPBR-GFP, or ARL4CΔPBR-GFP-Cterm.
source: In addition, inhibition of invasive ability by ARL4C ASO-1316 was cancelled by expression of ARL4CG2A-GFP-Cterm but not by that of ARL4CG2A-GFP, ARL4CΔPBR-GFP, or ARL4CΔPBR-GFP-Cterm (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The binding of ARL4C and IQGAP1 in invasive pseudopods could be essential for the invasive ability.
source: Thus, the binding of ARL4C and IQGAP1 in invasive pseudopods could be essential for the invasive ability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 (PIP2) and PI(3,4,5)P3 (PIP3) are required for ARL4C membrane targeting.
source: PI(4,5)P2 (PIP2) and PI(3,4,5)P3 (PIP3) are required for ARL4C membrane targeting (Heo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heo et al., 2006.

claim: GFP-PLCδPH was detected throughout the cell surface membrane, whereas GFP-GRP1PH was accumulated in invasive pseudopods.
source: GFP-PLCδPH was detected throughout the cell surface membrane, whereas GFP-GRP1PH was accumulated in invasive pseudopods (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PIP3 depletion decreased the membrane targeting of ARL4C and IQGAP1 and reduced the invasive ability, but PIP2 depletion did not.
source: PIP3 depletion decreased the membrane targeting of ARL4C and IQGAP1 and reduced the invasive ability, but PIP2 depletion did not (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B-C.

claim: IQGAP1 and ARL4C-mCherry colocalized with GRP1PH in invasive pseudopods.
source: IQGAP1 and ARL4C-mCherry colocalized with GRP1PH in invasive pseudopods (Figure 5D), suggesting that both proteins accumulate in the cell peripheral regions containing PIP3 and promote invasion.
evidence: This is supported by triple immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both ARL4C and IQGAP1 accumulate in the cell peripheral regions containing PIP3 and promote invasion.
source: IQGAP1 and ARL4C-mCherry colocalized with GRP1PH in invasive pseudopods (Figure 5D), suggesting that both proteins accumulate in the cell peripheral regions containing PIP3 and promote invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization data.

claim: Both ARL4CG2A-GFP-GRP1PH and ARL4CG2A-GFP-PLCδPH formed a complex with GFP-IQGAP1.
source: While both ARL4CG2A-GFP-GRP1PH and ARL4CG2A-GFP-PLCδPH formed a complex with GFP-IQGAP1, the former construct was localized to invasive pseudopods, but the latter construct was present throughout the cell surface membrane (Figure 5F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ARL4CG2A-GFP-GRP1PH was localized to invasive pseudopods, but ARL4CG2A-GFP-PLCδPH was present throughout the cell surface membrane.
source: While both ARL4CG2A-GFP-GRP1PH and ARL4CG2A-GFP-PLCδPH formed a complex with GFP-IQGAP1, the former construct was localized to invasive pseudopods, but the latter construct was present throughout the cell surface membrane (Figure 5F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In ARL4C KO cells extending invasive pseudopods, the localization of IQGAP1 to invasive pseudopods was rescued by ARL4CG2A-GFP-GRP1PH but not by ARL4CG2A-GFP-PLCδPH.
source: Consistently, in ARL4C KO cells extending invasive pseudopods, the localization of IQGAP1 to invasive pseudopods was rescued by ARL4CG2A-GFP-GRP1PH but not by ARL4CG2A-GFP-PLCδPH (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 inhibited the invasive ability of S2-CP8 cells expressing ARL4CG2A-GFP-PLCδPH but not those expressing ARL4CG2A-GFP-GRP1PH.
source: Furthermore, ARL4C ASO-1316 inhibited the invasive ability of S2-CP8 cells expressing ARL4CG2A-GFP-PLCδPH but not those expressing ARL4CG2A-GFP-GRP1PH (Figure 5H; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PIP3-dependent membrane targeting of ARL4C recruits IQGAP1 to invasive pseudopods and promotes invasion.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that PIP3-dependent membrane targeting of ARL4C recruits IQGAP1 to invasive pseudopods and promotes invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PH domain fusion experiments.

claim: IQGAP1 is involved in the trafficking of MMP14-containing vesicles to the leading structures of cancer cells.
source: IQGAP1 is involved in the trafficking of MMP14-containing vesicles to the leading structures of cancer cells (Sakurai-Yageta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sakurai-Yageta et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of MMP14 mRNA in pancreatic cancer patients is positively correlated with that of both ARL4C and IQGAP1 mRNA.
source: TCGA dataset showed that expression of MMP14 mRNA in pancreatic cancer patients is positively correlated with that of both ARL4C and IQGAP1 mRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MMP14 expression was associated with poor prognosis.
source: In addition, MMP14 expression was associated with poor prognosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cell surface MMP14-GFP accumulated in invasive pseudopods containing IQGAP1 and ARL4C-FLAG-HA.
source: Cell surface MMP14-GFP accumulated in invasive pseudopods containing IQGAP1 and ARL4C-FLAG-HA (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MMP14-GFP extremely disappeared from invasive pseudopods of ARL4C knockdown and KO cells and the phenotype was rescued by expression of ARL4C-FLAG-HA.
source: MMP14-GFP extremely disappeared from invasive pseudopods of ARL4C knockdown and KO cells and the phenotype was rescued by expression of ARL4C-FLAG-HA (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: IQGAP1 KO caused the loss of MMP14-GFP from the pseudopods, and FLAG-HA-IQGAP1 expression rescued this phenotype.
source: IQGAP1 KO caused the loss of MMP14-GFP from the pseudopods, and FLAG-HA-IQGAP1 expression rescued this phenotype (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The failure of MMP14 membrane targeting in ARL4C KO cells was rescued by expression of ARL4CG2A-FLAG-HA-Cterm but not by that of ARL4CG2A-FLAG-HA, ARL4CΔPBR-FLAG-HA, or ARL4CΔPBR-FLAG-HA-Cterm.
source: The failure of MMP14 membrane targeting in ARL4C KO cells was rescued by expression of ARL4CG2A-FLAG-HA-Cterm but not by that of ARL4CG2A-FLAG-HA, ARL4CΔPBR-FLAG-HA, or ARL4CΔPBR-FLAG-HA-Cterm (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PIP3 depletion, but not PIP2 depletion, suppressed the membrane localization of MMP14.
source: In addition, PIP3 depletion, but not PIP2 depletion, suppressed the membrane localization of MMP14 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In co-operation with ARL4C and IQGAP1, MMP14 is likely to be trafficked to invasive pseudopods with PIP3 accumulation.
source: Therefore, in co-operation with ARL4C and IQGAP1, MMP14 is likely to be trafficked to invasive pseudopods with PIP3 accumulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and rescue experiments.

claim: The inhibited invasive ability after double knockdown of ARL4C and MMP14 or IQGAP1 and MMP14 was similar to that seen after single knockdown of ARL4C, IQGAP1, or MMP14.
source: Consistent with these results, the inhibited invasive ability after double knockdown of ARL4C and MMP14 or IQGAP1 and MMP14 was similar to that seen after single knockdown of ARL4C, IQGAP1, or MMP14 (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Knockdown of ARL4C, IQGAP1, or MMP14 decreased invasive ability in 3D microfluidic cell culture.
source: Knockdown of ARL4C, IQGAP1, or MMP14 decreased invasive ability in 3D microfluidic cell culture (Figure 6F) and the protease activity was also reduced (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by 3D gel invasion assay data shown in Figures 6F-G.

claim: Knockdown of ARL4C, IQGAP1, or MMP14 reduced protease activity.
source: Knockdown of ARL4C, IQGAP1, or MMP14 decreased invasive ability in 3D microfluidic cell culture (Figure 6F) and the protease activity was also reduced (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by DQ-collagen degradation assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: MMP14ΔC(Δ563–582) lacking the cytoplasmic region fails to be endocytosed.
source: Previous work has shown that MMP14ΔC(Δ563–582) lacking the cytoplasmic region fails to be endocytosed (Jiang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2001.

claim: MMP14ΔC was retained in invasive pseudopods of ARL4C-KO cells.
source: Here, MMP14ΔC was retained in invasive pseudopods of ARL4C-KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G), and the ARL4C knockdown-mediated decreases in cell invasion and collagen degradation were rescued by MMP14ΔC (Figure 6H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The ARL4C knockdown-mediated decreases in cell invasion and collagen degradation were rescued by MMP14ΔC.
source: Here, MMP14ΔC was retained in invasive pseudopods of ARL4C-KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G), and the ARL4C knockdown-mediated decreases in cell invasion and collagen degradation were rescued by MMP14ΔC (Figure 6H; Figure 6—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: This is supported by invasion and DQ-collagen assay data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H-I.

claim: ARL4C-dependent recruitment of MMP14 to invasive pseudopods is required for cell invasion.
source: Thus, ARL4C-dependent recruitment of MMP14 to invasive pseudopods is required for cell invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments with MMP14ΔC.

claim: ARL4C and MMP14 were expressed more highly in invasive cancer cells rather than in PanIN lesions, although IQGAP1 was thoroughly expressed in tumor lesions including PanIN area.
source: Notably, ARL4C and MMP14 were expressed more highly in invasive cancer cells rather than in PanIN lesions, although IQGAP1 was thoroughly expressed in tumor lesions including PanIN area (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Three proteins (ARL4C, IQGAP1, and MMP14) are simultaneously expressed in PDAC cells invading the surrounding interstitial tissues.
source: Using triple immunofluorescence imaging assay, it was confirmed that three proteins are simultaneously expressed in PDAC cells invading the surrounding interstitial tissues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by triple immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling axis participates in pancreatic cancer cell invasion.
source: Taken together, these results support the idea that the ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling axis participates in pancreatic cancer cell invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental evidence.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 suppressed the luminescence signal compared with control ASO after 2 and 3 weeks.
source: After 2 and 3 weeks, ARL4C ASO-1316 suppressed the luminescence signal compared with control ASO (Figure 7B), and ARL4C expression was decreased immunohistochemically (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ARL4C expression was decreased immunohistochemically after ARL4C ASO-1316 treatment.
source: After 2 and 3 weeks, ARL4C ASO-1316 suppressed the luminescence signal compared with control ASO (Figure 7B), and ARL4C expression was decreased immunohistochemically (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 did not reduce the size of the primary tumor in the pancreas.
source: Whereas ARL4C ASO-1316 did not reduce the size of the primary tumor in the pancreas, the ASO decreased the numbers of lymph node metastases and tended to improve the survival (Figure 7D and E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor weight measurements shown in Figure 7E.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 decreased the numbers of lymph node metastases.
source: Whereas ARL4C ASO-1316 did not reduce the size of the primary tumor in the pancreas, the ASO decreased the numbers of lymph node metastases and tended to improve the survival (Figure 7D and E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by lymph node metastasis counts shown in Figure 7E.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 tended to improve the survival.
source: Whereas ARL4C ASO-1316 did not reduce the size of the primary tumor in the pancreas, the ASO decreased the numbers of lymph node metastases and tended to improve the survival (Figure 7D and E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 6-FAM–labeled ARL4C ASO-1316 was highly accumulated in tumor lesions but not in the neighboring normal tissues.
source: When 6-FAM–labeled ARL4C ASO-1316 was subcutaneously injected into tumor-bearing mice, the fluorescence was extremely detected in the pancreas and slightly observed in the kidney which is due to renal excretion (Figure 7F). 6-FAM–labeled ARL4C ASO-1316 was highly accumulated in tumor lesions but not in the neighboring normal tissues (Figure 7G), indicating that ASO was incorporated into tumor lesions after systemic injection.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figures 7F-G.

claim: ASO was incorporated into tumor lesions after systemic injection.
source: 6-FAM–labeled ARL4C ASO-1316 was highly accumulated in tumor lesions but not in the neighboring normal tissues (Figure 7G), indicating that ASO was incorporated into tumor lesions after systemic injection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence distribution data.

claim: In primary pancreatic tumors, ARL4C ASO-1316 reduced ARL4C expression at protein and mRNA levels.
source: In primary pancreatic tumors, ARL4C ASO-1316 reduced ARL4C expression at protein and mRNA levels (Figure 7H; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and decreased the localization of IQGAP1 to the cell surface area (Figure 7I; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ARL4C ASO-1316 decreased the localization of IQGAP1 to the cell surface area.
source: In primary pancreatic tumors, ARL4C ASO-1316 reduced ARL4C expression at protein and mRNA levels (Figure 7H; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and decreased the localization of IQGAP1 to the cell surface area (Figure 7I; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7I and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tumor cells were observed in lymphatic vessels of peritumoral areas of control ASO-treated mice but not in those of ARL4C ASO-treated mice.
source: Tumor cells were observed in lymphatic vessels of peritumoral areas of control ASO-treated mice but not in those of ARL4C ASO-treated mice (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Tumor cells surrounding peritumoral lymphatic vessels were also decreased.
source: In addition, tumor cells surrounding peritumoral lymphatic vessels were also decreased, which is consistent with our hypothesis that ARL4C is required for cell invasive activity.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations.

claim: Principal component analysis indicated a clear difference in the gene expression profiles of tumors from control ASO- and ARL4C ASO-1316–treated mice.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) indicated a clear difference in the gene expression profiles of tumors from control ASO- and ARL4C ASO-1316–treated mice (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq PCA data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed a drastic change in expression of genes due to ARL4C ASO-1316 injection.
source: Furthermore, hierarchical clustering revealed a drastic change in expression of genes due to ARL4C ASO-1316 injection (Figure 7L).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq clustering data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: DEGs linked to the inhibition of the pathways in ARL4C ASO-1316–treated mice were predicted to be involved in terms such as cell migration and invasion.
source: In particular, DEGs linked to the inhibition of the pathways in ARL4C ASO-1316–treated mice were predicted to be involved in terms such as cell migration and invasion (Figure 7M).
evidence: This is supported by IPA analysis shown in Figure 7M.

claim: ARL4C ASO inhibits the invasion of tumor cells into lymphatic vessels in vivo.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that ARL4C ASO inhibits the invasion of tumor cells into lymphatic vessels in vivo, and the gene profiles of tumors treated with ARL4C ASO in vivo support the putative functions of ARL4C in pancreatic cancer invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vivo experimental data.

claim: The gene profiles of tumors treated with ARL4C ASO in vivo support the putative functions of ARL4C in pancreatic cancer invasion.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that ARL4C ASO inhibits the invasion of tumor cells into lymphatic vessels in vivo, and the gene profiles of tumors treated with ARL4C ASO in vivo support the putative functions of ARL4C in pancreatic cancer invasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq and IPA analysis.

claim: ARL4C is constitutively active, regardless of wild-type.
source: ARL4C is a unique small G protein because it is constitutively active, regardless of wild-type (Burd et al., 2004; Matsumoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burd et al., 2004 and Matsumoto et al., 2017.

claim: The long interswitch region of ARL4C may prevent the retractile conformation change in the GDP-bound state.
source: The long interswitch region of ARL4C may prevent the retractile conformation change in the GDP-bound state (Burd et al., 2004; Pasqualato et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burd et al., 2004 and Pasqualato et al., 2002.

claim: ARL4C could be a constitutively active form without active mutations, and its activity may be controlled by transcriptional regulation.
source: ARL4C could be a constitutively active form without active mutations, and its activity may be controlled by transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and expression characteristics of ARL4C.

claim: ARL4C regulates different downstream signaling pathways in a cancer cell context-dependent manner.
source: Because ARL4C did not bind to cytohesin2 but to IQGAP1 in pancreatic cancer cells, it is likely that ARL4C regulates different downstream signaling pathways in a cancer cell context-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different binding partners in different cell types.

claim: Invadopodia are the unique structures observed at the ventral sites of certain types of cancer cells.
source: Invadopodia are the unique structures observed at the ventral sites of certain types of cancer cells, such as BxPC-3, breast cancer MDA-MB-231 cells, and head and neck squamous carcinoma SCC61 cells (Dalaka et al., 2020; Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011), but the typical invadopodia are not observed in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dalaka et al., 2020 and Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011.

claim: The typical invadopodia are not observed in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells.
source: Invadopodia are the unique structures observed at the ventral sites of certain types of cancer cells, such as BxPC-3, breast cancer MDA-MB-231 cells, and head and neck squamous carcinoma SCC61 cells (Dalaka et al., 2020; Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011), but the typical invadopodia are not observed in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Invasive pseudopods in S2-CP8 and PANC-1 cells consisted of similar molecules, including cortactin, ARPC2, IQGAP1, and MMP14, which are involved in invadopodia functions.
source: Invasive pseudopods that we defined in these pancreatic cancer cells highly expressing ARL4C consisted of similar molecules, including cortactin, ARPC2, IQGAP1, and MMP14, which are involved in invadopodia functions (Caswell and Zech, 2018; Jacquemet et al., 2013; Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and citations.

claim: Major function of ARL4C in invasive pseudopods would be to recruit MMP14 by binding to IQGAP1 rather than pseudopod formation.
source: ARL4C depletion severely suppresses the localization of IQGAP1 and MMP14 to pseudopods and inhibits invasive ability, but does affect the localization of cortactin as well as the structure itself only moderately. Therefore, major function of ARL4C in invasive pseudopods would be to recruit MMP14 by binding to IQGAP1 rather than pseudopod formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of ARL4C depletion on different pseudopod components.

claim: Both myristoylation and the PBR of ARL4C support plasma membrane targeting.
source: Both myristoylation and the PBR of ARL4C support plasma membrane targeting (Heo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heo et al., 2006.

claim: Both motifs (myristoylation and PBR) were necessary for the localization of ARL4C to the plasma membrane.
source: In our results, both motifs were necessary for the localization of ARL4C to the plasma membrane, whereas the PBR, rather than myristoylation, was indispensable for the activity of the ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling axis.
evidence: This is based on experimental data with ARL4C mutants.

claim: The PBR, rather than myristoylation, was indispensable for the activity of the ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling axis.
source: In our results, both motifs were necessary for the localization of ARL4C to the plasma membrane, whereas the PBR, rather than myristoylation, was indispensable for the activity of the ARL4C–IQGAP1–MMP14 signaling axis.
evidence: This is based on experimental data with ARL4C mutants.

claim: PIP3 is localized to the leading edge of migrating cells and invadopodia of cancer cells.
source: PIP3 is localized to the leading edge of migrating cells and invadopodia of cancer cells (Saykali and El-Sibai, 2014) and recruits cytosolic proteins containing lipid-binding domains, such as the PH domain, to the plasma membrane (Toker and Cantley, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saykali and El-Sibai, 2014 and Toker and Cantley, 1997.

claim: PIP3 recruits cytosolic proteins containing lipid-binding domains, such as the PH domain, to the plasma membrane.
source: PIP3 is localized to the leading edge of migrating cells and invadopodia of cancer cells (Saykali and El-Sibai, 2014) and recruits cytosolic proteins containing lipid-binding domains, such as the PH domain, to the plasma membrane (Toker and Cantley, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Toker and Cantley, 1997.

claim: ARL4C in pancreatic cancer cells preferred PIP3 to PIP2.
source: ARL4C in pancreatic cancer cells preferred PIP3 to PIP2.
evidence: This is based on experimental data with PIP2 and PIP3 depletion.

claim: PI3 kinase is one of the direct effector proteins of RAS.
source: Because PI3 kinase is one of the direct effector proteins of RAS (Castellano and Downward, 2011; Rodriguez-Viciana et al., 1994), RAS-dependent PI3 kinase activation and ARL4C expression could co-operatively function to promote pancreatic cancer invasion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Castellano and Downward, 2011 and Rodriguez-Viciana et al., 1994.

claim: RAS-dependent PI3 kinase activation and ARL4C expression could co-operatively function to promote pancreatic cancer invasion.
source: Because PI3 kinase is one of the direct effector proteins of RAS (Castellano and Downward, 2011; Rodriguez-Viciana et al., 1994), RAS-dependent PI3 kinase activation and ARL4C expression could co-operatively function to promote pancreatic cancer invasion.
evidence: This is speculation based on the relationship between RAS, PI3K, PIP3, and ARL4C.

claim: Invasion of pancreatic cancer cells is promoted by ARL4C, of which expression is induced by KRAS and Wnt signaling.
source: In conclusion, this study clarified that invasion of pancreatic cancer cells is promoted by ARL4C, of which expression is induced by KRAS and Wnt signaling, and that association of ARL4C with IQGAP1 and MMP14 at the tips of invasive pseudopods are essential for the invasive ability.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Association of ARL4C with IQGAP1 and MMP14 at the tips of invasive pseudopods are essential for the invasive ability.
source: In conclusion, this study clarified that invasion of pancreatic cancer cells is promoted by ARL4C, of which expression is induced by KRAS and Wnt signaling, and that association of ARL4C with IQGAP1 and MMP14 at the tips of invasive pseudopods are essential for the invasive ability.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The novel functions of ARL4C were confirmed by the mouse model.
source: The novel functions of ARL4C were confirmed by the mouse model.
evidence: This is based on the in vivo orthotopic transplantation experiments.

claim: The inhibition of ARL4C expression by ARL4C ASO could directly inhibit invasive ability of pancreatic cancer cells.
source: The inhibition of ARL4C expression by ARL4C ASO could directly inhibit invasive ability of pancreatic cancer cells and may indirectly affect the genes involved in invasion perhaps through the interaction between tumors and surrounding tissues.
evidence: This is based on the in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: The inhibition of ARL4C expression by ARL4C ASO may indirectly affect the genes involved in invasion perhaps through the interaction between tumors and surrounding tissues.
source: The inhibition of ARL4C expression by ARL4C ASO could directly inhibit invasive ability of pancreatic cancer cells and may indirectly affect the genes involved in invasion perhaps through the interaction between tumors and surrounding tissues.
evidence: This is speculation based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: Histological damage to the non-tumor regions was not observed after the administration of ARL4C ASO-1316.
source: Because histological damage to the non-tumor regions was not observed after the administration of ARL4C ASO-1316 (Harada et al., 2019), ARL4C might represent an appropriate target for pancreatic cancer therapy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harada et al., 2019.

claim: ARL4C might represent an appropriate target for pancreatic cancer therapy.
source: Because histological damage to the non-tumor regions was not observed after the administration of ARL4C ASO-1316 (Harada et al., 2019), ARL4C might represent an appropriate target for pancreatic cancer therapy.
evidence: This is speculation based on the safety and efficacy data.

claim: ARL4C is frequently expressed in atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, which is the possible precursor lesions and develops to lung adenocarcinoma.
source: The results are consistent with our recent observations that ARL4C is frequently expressed in atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, which is the possible precursor lesions and develops to lung adenocarcinoma (Kimura et al., 2020).
